## How to write the story and scene

### Story

Write the full text the learner will read. Begin with a situation, observation, or puzzle that gives them a reason to ask the question. Let the question develop through what happens next. Introduce a term when the learner needs it, and use a concrete example or a calculation where it helps them picture what is happening. Include the origin of an idea when it helps explain where the question or mechanism comes from.

Build toward an ending that resolves the opening question. A story can follow a person noticing something, a real experiment, or a problem unfolding in its own setting. Dialogue and fictional characters are optional. Keep the whole story in the table, including the setup, the discovery, and the ending.

### What the scene shows

Design a visual experiment from the story’s important events and relationships. Describe what appears first, what changes or gets compared, what the learner can observe, and which final view answers the question. Identify the visual components and what each represents. In the tennis example, the ball is an SVG glyph, the toss starts at a launch mark, and the opening hand becomes a release gate.

Explain the layout and the visual evidence in enough detail for someone to build the scene. Name the objects, paths, arrows, labels, guides, plots, and measurements that matter. State which marks share a scale, which quantities are compared, and what stays visible as the experiment advances. If two moments have the same position but different velocities, describe how the scene makes that distinction visible. Describe new components when the experiment needs them.

### Expectations by depth

| Depth | Story | What the scene shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Brief** | Start from a familiar situation and resolve one clear question. Introduce essential terms in plain language as the story needs them. Use a small example that helps the reader picture the result. | Build one clear comparison. Establish the starting state, show the important difference or change, and end with visible evidence for the answer. Use simple shapes and labels to make the relationship easy to read. |
| **Balanced** | Explain the mechanism through a worked example. Follow the important steps in order, explain what each quantity means, and use concrete values when they clarify the change. Return to the opening question with a causal explanation. | Make the mechanism observable. Specify the states or instants being compared, the scale, and the arrows or readouts that change. Keep the relevant invariant visible so the learner can distinguish what changes from what drives the change. |
| **Detailed** | Investigate why the result holds and under which assumptions. Derive or trace the governing relationship, work through its consequences, and resolve the original observation or an apparent contradiction. Use a contrasting case or boundary when it adds insight. | Make the reasoning inspectable. Choose measurements, diagrams, linked plots, or magnified views that expose the relationship. Specify units, reference points, and which quantities stay fixed. A controlled comparison can show what changes when an assumption or input changes. |

## How to define Mode and Controls

### Mode

The **Mode** column specifies how the experiment runs. Choose the mode from the scene’s timeline and the inputs the learner can change. Each depth can use any of the three modes.

| Mode | Timeline | Learner-adjustable scene parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Static** | None. The scene shows one or more still states. | Optional. Changing a parameter updates the still state. |
| **Over time** | Present. The scene follows a fixed sequence. | None. The experiment’s parameters are fixed. |
| **Interact** | Present. The scene follows a sequence that depends on the learner’s input. | At least one parameter changes how the experiment unfolds. |

Play, pause, replay, and scrubbing are timeline actions. For mode selection, count inputs that change the experiment itself, such as launch speed.

In the Mode cell, record the initial state, fixed values, assumptions, and quantities the learner can change. For a scene with a timeline, specify what time measures, its start and end, and the events at important instants. Describe what play, pause, replay, and scrubbing do, including which views update together. If a scene parameter changes, explain how the experiment recalculates and whether playback resumes or returns to a defined state.

### Controls

The **Controls** column maps the behavior in Mode to specific UI elements. Give each element’s visible label and type, such as a button, slider, selector, or timeline scrubber. Include the applicable units, default, minimum, maximum, step, or discrete options. For a scrubber, include its displayed range and marker labels. For a button that changes labels, map each label to its state.

For example, **Launch speed** maps to a slider in metres per second with a default of **5.0 m/s**, a range of **3.0–5.0 m/s**, and a step of **0.1 m/s**. The effect of changing launch speed belongs in **Mode**. Use **None** when a scene has no UI controls.

## The scene family (depth brief)
Family vertical-throw: a ball thrown straight up; up is positive; no air resistance; the card is an experiment with Play, a scrubber, an At top button and Reset.
At depth brief: One lane (template one-body): one ball thrown up from a launch mark on a fixed height scale, a Motion arrow for its velocity (absent at the top), a constant gravity arrow and a callout naming the motion.
The timeline starts at launch and ends when the ball is back at its launch height (2 * launchSpeed / gravity); it pauses at the top (where the velocity is zero) and, in the two-lane and plot depths, 0.10 s before and after it.
Inputs the reader changes: launch speed (gravity is fixed). Each has a minimum, a maximum, a default and a step.
Write the physics as formulas over t and those input names, and the words the card shows (headings, state lines, callout lines) in the limits given.

## The keys of the plan brief
- title: the card title (at most 120 characters)
- story: a short story that motivates the question, a few short paragraphs (at most 3000 characters)
- cardDescription: two to four lines under the title: the idea of the card, with $...$ for maths (at most 500 characters)
- instructions: two or three short sentences: what to change and press (at most 300 characters)
- launchHeight: height of the launch mark above the ground mark in metres (0 when the ball is thrown from the ground mark)
- launchSpeed: Launch speed, m/s. Upward speed at the instant of the throw. Measured at the launch mark, up is positive. (range: min, max, default, step)
- gravity: Gravity, m/s^2. Magnitude of the constant downward acceleration. Idealized, no air resistance. (one number, fixed)
- formulas.height: Height of the ball, m. Height above the ground mark, up positive; the launch height is its value at t = 0.
- formulas.velocity: Vertical velocity, m/s. Signed rate of change of height, up positive; zero at the top.
- formulas.acceleration: Vertical acceleration, m/s^2. Signed rate of change of velocity: constant and negative (down), -gravity.
- formulas.apexTime: Time of the top, s. Elapsed time from launch at which the velocity is zero.
- formulas.apexHeight: Height of the top, m. Height of the ball at its top above the ground mark.
- words.lane: heading of the lane (at most 24 characters)
- words.launch: label of the launch-height guide (at most 40 characters)
- words.gravity_pulls: callout line while gravity pulls the body down (at most 40 characters)
- words.gravity_none: callout line when nothing pulls (at most 40 characters)
- words.motion_up: callout line while the body moves up (at most 40 characters)
- words.motion_top: callout line while the body is still for an instant at the top (at most 40 characters)
- words.motion_down: callout line while the body moves down (at most 40 characters)
- words.where_launch: lane state at launch (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_top: lane state at the top (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_end: lane state when back at the launch height (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_up: lane state while rising (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_down: lane state while falling (at most 32 characters)
- words.readout_motion: label of the Motion state readout (at most 24 characters)
- words.readout_gravity: label of the Gravity state readout (at most 24 characters)

## Limits
title: at most 120 characters. story: at most 3000 characters. instructions: at most 300 characters.
cardDescription: exactly two sentences of 130 to 200 characters in all, one plain paragraph with no line break and no markdown (under 130 characters is one line and is refused; so is anything over 4 lines; never split it with a line break).
Every word is at most the number of characters its key states.
A formula reads only the names t, launchSpeed, gravity; any other name (height, velocity, acceleration, apexTime, apexHeight, launchHeight) is refused.

## Formulas
A formula is text: numbers, names, + - * /, unary minus, parentheses, and ^ with a literal whole-number exponent 2, 3 or 4 (for example t^2). Nothing else: no functions, no conditions, no other powers. At most 200 characters and 32 nodes.
The readable names are `t` (elapsed seconds since launch, 0 at the launch), the scene's numeric inputs by id (launchSpeed, gravity, mass where the scene has them) and, where the scene fixes gravity, `gravity`. Up is positive; a force is a magnitude. A quantity that changes rule at one moment is piecewise: `formula` applies while t < switchAt, `formulaAfter` from switchAt on; switchAt is a formula over the inputs only (no t). Give switchAt and formulaAfter as null when the quantity has one rule at every time.
launchHeight is a number: write it as a literal, never as a name in a formula.
A formula has at most 32 nodes.
The detailed timeline counts time from the launch, and a marker is never before 0.

Return the brief only: no prose.

If two moments have the same position but different velocities, describe how the scene makes that distinction visible. Describe new components when the experiment needs them.

### Expectations by depth

| Depth | Story | What the scene shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Brief** | Start from a familiar situation and resolve one clear question. Introduce essential terms in plain language as the story needs them. Use a small example that helps the reader picture the result. | Build one clear comparison. Establish the starting state, show the important difference or change, and end with visible evidence for the answer. Use simple shapes and labels to make the relationship easy to read. |
| **Balanced** | Explain the mechanism through a worked example. Follow the important steps in order, explain what each quantity means, and use concrete values when they clarify the change. Return to the opening question with a causal explanation. | Make the mechanism observable. Specify the states or instants being compared, the scale, and the arrows or readouts that change. Keep the relevant invariant visible so the learner can distinguish what changes from what drives the change. |
| **Detailed** | Investigate why the result holds and under which assumptions. Derive or trace the governing relationship, work through its consequences, and resolve the original observation or an apparent contradiction. Use a contrasting case or boundary when it adds insight. | Make the reasoning inspectable. Choose measurements, diagrams, linked plots, or magnified views that expose the relationship. Specify units, reference points, and which quantities stay fixed. A controlled comparison can show what changes when an assumption or input changes. |

## How to define Mode and Controls

### Mode

The **Mode** column specifies how the experiment runs. Choose the mode from the scene’s timeline and the inputs the learner can change. Each depth can use any of the three modes.

| Mode | Timeline | Learner-adjustable scene parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Static** | None. The scene shows one or more still states. | Optional. Changing a parameter updates the still state. |
| **Over time** | Present. The scene follows a fixed sequence. | None. The experiment’s parameters are fixed. |
| **Interact** | Present. The scene follows a sequence that depends on the learner’s input. | At least one parameter changes how the experiment unfolds. |

Play, pause, replay, and scrubbing are timeline actions. For mode selection, count inputs that change the experiment itself, such as launch speed.

In the Mode cell, record the initial state, fixed values, assumptions, and quantities the learner can change. For a scene with a timeline, specify what time measures, its start and end, and the events at important instants. Describe what play, pause, replay, and scrubbing do, including which views update together. If a scene parameter changes, explain how the experiment recalculates and whether playback resumes or returns to a defined state.

### Controls

The **Controls** column maps the behavior in Mode to specific UI elements. Give each element’s visible label and type, such as a button, slider, selector, or timeline scrubber. Include the applicable units, default, minimum, maximum, step, or discrete options. For a scrubber, include its displayed range and marker labels. For a button that changes labels, map each label to its state.

For example, **Launch speed** maps to a slider in metres per second with a default of **5.0 m/s**, a range of **3.0–5.0 m/s**, and a step of **0.1 m/s**. The effect of changing launch speed belongs in **Mode**. Use **None** when a scene has no UI controls.

## The scene family (depth detailed)
Family vertical-throw: a ball thrown straight up; up is positive; no air resistance; the card is an experiment with Play, a scrubber, an At top button and Reset.

## The keys of the plan brief
- title: the card title (at most 120 characters)
- story: a short story that motivates the question, a few short paragraphs (at most 3000 characters)
- cardDescription: two to four lines under the title: the idea of the card, with $...$ for maths (at most 500 characters)
- instructions: two or three short sentences: what to change and press (at most 300 characters)
- launchHeight: height of the launch mark above the ground mark in metres (0 when the ball is thrown from the ground mark)
- launchSpeed: Launch speed, m/s. Upward speed at the instant of the throw. Measured at the launch mark, up is positive. (range: min, max, default, step)
- gravity: Gravity, m/s^2. Magnitude of the constant downward acceleration. Idealized, no air resistance. (range: min, max, default, step)
- mass: Mass, kg. Mass of the ball. Does not change the motion. (range: min, max, default, step)
- formulas.height: Height of the ball, m. Height above the ground mark, up positive; the launch height is its value at t = 0.
- formulas.velocity: Vertical velocity, m/s. Signed rate of change of height, up positive; zero at the top.
- formulas.acceleration: Vertical acceleration, m/s^2. Signed rate of change of velocity: constant and negative (down), -gravity.
- formulas.force: Gravitational force, N. Magnitude of the downward force of gravity on the ball (positive, the arrow draws it down).
- formulas.apexTime: Time of the top, s. Elapsed time from launch at which the velocity is zero.
- formulas.apexHeight: Height of the top, m. Height of the ball at its top above the ground mark.
- words.lane: heading of the lane (at most 24 characters)
- words.launch: label of the launch-height guide (at most 40 characters)
- words.axis_label: title of the height axis (at most 40 characters)
- words.v: letter beside the velocity arrow (at most 4 characters)
- words.a: letter beside the acceleration arrow (at most 4 characters)
- words.force: letter of the force in its callout line (at most 4 characters)
- words.where_launch: lane state at launch (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_top: lane state at the top (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_end: lane state when back at the launch height (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_up: lane state while rising (at most 32 characters)
- words.where_down: lane state while falling (at most 32 characters)
- words.plot_heading: heading of the plot (at most 40 characters)
- words.plot_yLabel: title of the plot value axis (at most 40 characters)
- words.plot_line: legend label of the plotted line (at most 40 characters)
- words.plot_now: legend label of the moving dot (at most 40 characters)
- words.plot_slope: start of the slope note (a number follows it) (at most 24 characters)
- words.plot_eq: start of the equation beside the heading (numbers follow it) (at most 24 characters)
- words.readout_motion: label of the Motion state readout (at most 24 characters)

## Limits
title: at most 120 characters. story: at most 3000 characters. instructions: at most 300 characters.
cardDescription: exactly two sentences of 130 to 200 characters in all, one plain paragraph with no line break and no markdown (under 130 characters is one line and is refused; so is anything over 4 lines; never split it with a line break).
Every word is at most the number of characters its key states.
A formula reads only the names t, launchSpeed, gravity, mass; any other name (height, velocity, acceleration, force, apexTime, apexHeight, launchHeight) is refused.

## Formulas
A formula is text: numbers, names, + - * /, unary minus, parentheses, and ^ with a literal whole-number exponent 2, 3 or 4 (for example t^2). Nothing else: no functions, no conditions, no other powers. At most 200 characters and 32 nodes.
The readable names are `t` (elapsed seconds since launch, 0 at the launch), the scene's numeric inputs by id (launchSpeed, gravity, mass where the scene has them) and, where the scene fixes gravity, `gravity`. Up is positive; a force is a magnitude. A quantity that changes rule at one moment is piecewise: `formula` applies while t < switchAt, `formulaAfter` from switchAt on; switchAt is a formula over the inputs only (no t). Give switchAt and formulaAfter as null when the quantity has one rule at every time.
launchHeight is a number: write it as a literal, never as a name in a formula.
A formula has at most 32 nodes.
The detailed timeline counts time from the launch, and a marker is never before 0.
words.lane plus its longest state word (words.where_*) is at most 25 characters in all; they share one line and a longer state word is cut on the card.
gravity: every value of its range is at least 4 (a smaller gravity draws no acceleration arrow and the card is refused). Every marker time is at least 0.
